item.title: Angel Reese reveals 'embarrassing' training camp story after reaching WNBA Finals with Atlanta Dream
item.description: Angel Reese revealed a training camp drill where Coach Karl Smesko forced her to hit two consecutive 3-pointers before the team could continue.
item.content:encoded:
Angel Reese has officially reached the WNBA Finals before Caitlin Clark, and gave fans a peek into the process that got her there after finishing off a three-game sweep of the New York Liberty in the semifinals on Friday, which included a training camp exercise that left her feeling "embarrassed' in front of her new Atlanta Dream teammates.

In the postgame news conference, Reese spoke about a moment in training-camp when Coach Karl Smesko stopped a drill and made her hit two consecutive 3-pointers before her teammates could continue.

Reese said the exercise left her upset with Smesko and worried about embarrassing herself in front of the team.

"It's really hard for me to not want to rush success, and Karl told me how patient I had to be with it. I remember a very moment in training camp where we were going through drills and he stopped everybody and told me I had to make two in a row in front of everybody," Reese said.

"And you never want to shutdown your teammates, you never want to let your teammates down, and we couldn't resume the drill until I made two in a row, and I was upset with him that day for sure. Because I didn't want to let the team down, I didn't want to feel embarrassed and in how long it coulda took me to make them. But now it's like so easy."

ANGEL REESE SETS TWO WNBA RECORDS WITH HISTORIC REBOUNDING PERFORMANCE

Reese is known as a poor shooter, and is often mocked for missing easy shots in games. She has even gotten in on the jokes herself by launching merchandise under the brand "Mebounds" in 2025. The term is a mocking play on "rebounds," referring to the rebounds she collects after missing her own shots.

Later in Friday's postgame news conference, Reese was asked how many shots she needed to make two consecutively.

"I don't know," Reese answered.

"It wasn't that many," Smesko said.

"My teammates are cheering for me on the sideline, and I was pretty embarrassed," Reese added.

Now, months later, she made two 3-pointers in Atlanta’s 85-83 victory over the New York Liberty, which completed a semifinal sweep and sent the Dream to their first Finals since 2013.

Her recollection addressed an area of her game that has attracted scrutiny throughout her professional career. Reese publicly pushed back against criticism of her missed layups in November 2024, following a rookie season in which she made 39.1% of her shots.

Her shooting numbers since then show progress from that rookie season, with a more modest change during her first year in Atlanta. Reese made 45.1% of her shots this regular season, slightly below the 45.8% she made in her second season with Chicago.

She attempted 3-pointers more frequently with the Dream, but still made fewer than one in five during the regular season. Her 19.3% success rate from beyond the arc was only slightly above last year’s 18.2%.

She has made five of 13 playoff 3-point attempts (38.5%). That represents a stronger stretch across just five games.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Reese’s overall production grew in Atlanta. She averaged a career-high 16.4 points, again led the WNBA in rebounding and won her first Defensive Player of the Year award. She finished Friday’s clinching victory with 22 points and nine rebounds.

The opportunity followed an April trade that sent Reese from Chicago to Atlanta for two first-round draft picks, with the Dream also receiving a future second-round pick swap. Chicago missed the playoffs in both of her seasons there and finished 10-34 in 2025.

Atlanta already had a franchise-record 30-win season behind it and retained a core that included All-Star guards Allisha Gray and Rhyne Howard and two-time WNBA champion Jordin Canada. Reese joined an established playoff team in Smesko’s second season as coach.

The Dream matched that 30-14 record this year and earned the fourth seed, giving them home-court advantage against Washington in the first round and New York in the semifinals. Sixth-seeded Indiana drew defending champion Las Vegas immediately and lost the deciding game on the road.

The Finals berth came despite Atlanta losing center Brionna Jones to a season-ending leg injury and playing the final two games against New York without Gray, who had a left hand injury.

Clark, who entered the WNBA alongside Reese in 2024, reached the playoffs first, during their rookie season. She missed the entire 2025 postseason with an injury, when Indiana eliminated Atlanta before falling one win short of the Finals against Las Vegas.

This year, Clark averaged a career-high 22.3 points and helped lead the highest-scoring offense in WNBA history alongside Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston. Indiana finished 28-16 before its first-round elimination.

Reese will now pursue her first WNBA championship, with the Finals scheduled to begin Oct. 17. Atlanta is seeking its first title in franchise history.

item.title: Sophie Cunningham responds to column urging Fever to move on from her for sharing opinions
item.description: Sophie Cunningham fired back at The Athletic's column urging the Indiana Fever to move on, as her co-host disputed its basketball arguments.
item.content:encoded:
Sophie Cunningham had a blunt response after a New York Times column urged the Indiana Fever to part ways with her:

"Suck it."

The Fever guard addressed the criticism on Friday’s episode of "No Hesitation with Sophie Cunningham & Drew Hanlen," pushing back against questions about her basketball value while saying she no longer lets outside opinions dictate how she lives.

"That’s why I literally don’t even care what anyone says about me anymore," Cunningham said. "Because I’ve said this so many times, is if you’re going to live by the praise, you’re going to die by the hate."

The discussion followed an Oct. 6 column by New York Times-owned The Athletic arguing that Indiana should move on from Cunningham. The column contended that the attention surrounding the guard’s outspoken views had overwhelmed the team’s basketball priorities, describing her as "too combustible." Cunningham is headed toward unrestricted free agency after two seasons with Indiana.

Her opposition to transgender athletes competing in girls’ and women’s sports became a major flashpoint this season, prompting demonstrations supporting and opposing her position outside the Fever games. Cunningham previously said she was not concerned that those rallies would distract her team.

Cunningham's co-host Hanlen called the column an "absolute hate piece," but said he wanted to focus his response on its basketball arguments.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT ON PROTECTING GIRLS FROM COMPETING AGAINST 'BIOLOGICAL MEN'

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

He disputed the suggestion that Cunningham’s scoring average diminished her appeal to other teams, saying she ranked fourth among the WNBA’s bench scorers and was a top-five three-point shooter.

"So yes, a lot of teams would want a top five bench scorer that also happens to be a top five three-point shooter in the entire league, not just bench players," Hanlen said.

He also challenged a passage discussing Cunningham’s effectiveness, citing her 60.8% effective field goal percentage and saying it ranked fourth in the league.

"I understand if you just don’t like somebody and you try to write a hate piece, but don’t try to kind of put down the basketball stuff," Hanlen said. "At least keep it with the facts."

Cunningham averaged 7.9 points, 2.3 rebounds and 1.2 assists during the regular season. She shot 41.9% from three-point range across 43 appearances, starting three games.

The column's fuller passage acknowledged Cunningham’s value as a protective teammate, saying her effectiveness "didn’t shine on a traditional stat sheet."

FEVER 2026 TIMELINE: HOW CAITLIN CLARK, SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AND RIVALS LIKELY CHANGED THE WNBA FOREVER

Cunningham maintained that her contribution extends beyond those numbers.

"No matter what anyone says to me, I’m going to continue to do me. I know what I bring to the table. It’s not always in the stat sheet," she said.

"And so for you to like not say I’m effective or any of that, whatever. Suck it."

item.title: Philadelphia police officers shot 15 times combined in ambush attack, suspect found hiding in tree
item.description: Two Philadelphia police officers were ambushed and shot multiple times on North 52nd Street. Kevin Bethel says one officer was hit 12 times.
item.content:encoded:
Two Philadelphia police officers are in the hospital after being shot early Saturday while responding to a call in the western part of the city.

One officer, a 40-year-old who has two children, was shot three times, Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel said during a news conference.

The other officer, a 33-year-old who has five children, was shot 12 times, Bethel said.

CONNECTICUT POLICE OFFICERS SHOT, SUSPECT KILLED AFTER ATTEMPTED ARREST SPARKS HECTIC CHASE

"I am so damn proud of the men and women who serve in this department. Consistently, they go into danger, and they give their lives for this job," Bethel told reporters. "And so we ask for those prayers, and we ask for you to support our men and women out there, and what they give for this profession."

Just after 12:20 a.m., the officers were dispatched to 140 North 52nd Street following a report of a man with a gun on a porch, Bethel said.

About 30 minutes later, the officers arrived at the address and came under "significant gunfire" once they were on the porch.

Shortly after shots were fired, Bethel said additional officers and a SWAT team found the original responding officers on the porch with gunshot wounds.

CHICAGO OFFICERS WOUNDED IN TRAFFIC STOP SHOOTOUT AS HOLIDAY WEEKEND LEAVES 3 DEAD, 16 INJURED

The suspect fired at two additional officers, Bethel said, but the SWAT team was able to locate the man in a tree and take him into custody.

The officers who were shot were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center for surgery. Their conditions are not clear.

"We are praying now that our officers make it through this terrible situation," Bethel said.

The suspect reportedly ambushed the officers by running down an alley and shooting at them, local outlet WPVI reported.

The suspect, whose name has not yet been released, was found with two handguns and a shotgun, Bethel said. One of the handguns belonged to one of the officers who had been shot.

The Philadelphia Police Department did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Fetterman plays political maverick, but his voting record tells another story
item.description: John Fetterman votes with Democrats a majority of the time, yet his Israel stance and Republican friendships fuel intense party-switch speculation.
item.content:encoded:
The Senate's most recognizable rogue Democrat has increasingly broken with his party since Republicans took control of the upper chamber, but he still votes with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., a majority of the time. 

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., is the Senate’s biggest enigma during a time of hyper-partisanship — he bucks his party on key issues, like the war in Iran and immigration, but continues to vote with Democrats an overwhelming amount of the time.

Since joining the Senate in 2023, Fetterman has voted with Senate Democrats nearly 90% of the time, a figure that stacks up closely to some of the most staunch party liners in the caucus. Still, speculation has swirled as to whether he'll jump the political shark and become a Republican. 

MAVERICK DEMOCRAT SURGES WITH REPUBLICANS AS HIS OWN PARTY TURNS ON HIM, STOKING TALK OF GOP SWITCH

Despite that, Fetterman has set the terms clearly this year, arguing that if Democrats continued to turn their backs on Israel, he would leave the party. But some in the GOP believe that no matter the swirl percolating in Washington, D.C., Fetterman isn’t swapping jerseys. He’s also keeping the speculation heavy about whether he will run for another term.

"John Fetterman is a staunch Democrat that votes with his party 96% of the time, anybody who seriously believes that he is going to switch to the Republican Party is thinking wishfully," a senior Republican aide told Fox News Digital.

Fetterman’s national political career began as a politician armed with an endorsement for Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., running in a pivotal race in 2022 against Dr. Mehmet Oz.

SEN JOHN FETTERMAN PLEDGES TO BE 'LAST MAN STANDING' IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN SUPPORT OF ISRAEL

Sanders told the Associated Press at the time that "if there’s any candidate who was running more than anybody else, who identified with the working class, who made it clear that he was going to Washington to represent working people, it was John Fetterman."

He flipped that seat, giving Democrats one of the slimmest majorities in history and cementing himself as a rock star in the party.

Since then, he’s run away from Sanders’ ideals and often rejected Schumer and the caucus’ marching orders.

But this year he’s leaned into that grey area, sometimes known as being a centrist, to support Republican ideals. During this session of Congress, Fetterman has broken from Democrats more than ever before, dropping to just under 81% along Democratic Party lines. 

And while that's happening, Fetterman is reportedly using Republican fundraising platforms to soak up precious donor dollars, is close friends with one of the GOP’s own rock stars, Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., made a video message introducing McCormick at the RNC and even accidentally called himself a lifelong Republican during an appearance at the Texas Tribune’s Tribfest last month.

FETTERMAN TEASES WHERE HIS TRUE LOYALTY LIES AFTER SURPRISE APPEARANCE AT GOP CONVENTION

But when asked about whether he’s considering leaving the party, even after drawing a line in the sand, he recoils — it’s become such a hot topic in the hallways of the Senate that Fetterman stopped taking questions.

As to whether he would jump ship depending on the outcome of the upcoming election, Fetterman said during the event that "there are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party."

"How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterms and see what happens," Fetterman said. "And now, if we do win, and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania."

Fetterman’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Michael Douglas' wildest Hollywood confessions: From A-list actress bite to Julia Roberts clash
item.description: Michael Douglas alleges a confrontation with Julia Roberts, secret affairs and a cocaine-fueled evening with O.J. Simpson in his new memoir.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Douglas is pulling back the curtain on the most explosive moments of his life, both in front of the camera and behind the scenes.

In his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the actor-producer also opens up about secret affairs, heavy cocaine and alcohol use, a "rehab or divorce" ultimatum from his first wife, Diandra, and the painful family struggles that followed him from childhood into fatherhood. 

Douglas details his volatile relationship with his late father, Kirk Douglas, his son Cameron’s addiction and imprisonment, and the stage IV cancer diagnosis that forced him to confront his own mortality.

Here are the top ten bombshells:

MICHAEL DOUGLAS CONFIRMS SECRET AFFAIR WITH KATHLEEN TURNER ON 'ROMANCING THE STONE' SET

In the book, Douglas recalled that he and the filmmakers were trying to convince Debra Winger to star as Joan Wilder in "Romancing the Stone," but the meeting took an odd turn.

"We took Debra to dinner and, once again, it was an epic meal. Any time you have dinner with Jack or Danny, it’s a riot. … But the real goal of the dinner was to get Debra on board to make Romancing the Stone, and no matter how hard we tried, she would not give us an answer, one way or the other. We were stuck in limbo."

MICHAEL DOUGLAS ADMITS HE ALMOST LEFT HIS WIFE FOR HIS 'BASIC INSTINCT' CO-STAR AFTER AFFAIR

"Stories had filtered back that Debra was delivering an incredible performance in Terms of Endearment, but also that she was difficult during shooting and had huge, blow-out fights with Shirley MacLaine," he wrote.

"We all left the restaurant and were walking down the street when, the way somebody might punch you in the arm as you part company, Debra leaned over and bit me. I mean, she really bit me. Jesus, I had a whole set of teeth marks dug into my arm. We still had no answer from her, but that bite sealed the deal for me. No, thank you!"

MICHAEL DOUGLAS REVEALS HE MADE FIVE PHONE CALLS TO FIVE WOMEN THE DAY HE CHOSE CATHERINE ZETA-JONES

Douglas said he later reenacted the moment for Fox executives, telling them, "She bit me. Hard. Look at the teeth marks in my arm."

Although the studio pushed back because Winger was a major star, Douglas held his ground. Winger ultimately did not join the project, and Kathleen Turner was cast in the role.

Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Winger for comment.

Douglas experienced another tense moment involving Julia Roberts at a Golden Globes party.

Douglas was at the event with his son Cameron, who was about 13 at the time. In the book, Douglas alleges that Roberts had her arm around Cameron and was "kind of nuzzling him." Douglas, who admits he was drunk, claims Cameron looked stunned.

BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG

"I told her, ‘Take your hands off my son and take that Golden Globe and stick it where the sun don’t shine,’" he writes.

Douglas later apologized to Roberts and her then-boyfriend, Kiefer Sutherland.

BRAD PITT ADMITS HE BEGAN DRINKING AGAIN AFTER YEARS OF SOBRIETY

"I sent Julia roses with an apology for my behavior, and then back in the production office, I apologized to her and Kiefer in person," he wrote.

Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Roberts for comment. 

While filming "Adam at 6 A.M." early in his career, Douglas says he and his married co-star Lee Purcell became lovers.

"As filming progressed, my relationship with Lee changed and we became lovers," he writes. "Our intimate relationship was complicated by the fact that she was married, and we had to keep it a secret from the cast, crew, the people in the town we were filming in, and of course her husband. It was a passionate affair that lasted through filming."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Years later, while making "Romancing the Stone," Douglas also admits he had an affair with screenwriter Diane Thomas, who wrote the film. He says he and his first wife, Diandra, were both involved in extramarital relationships as their marriage deteriorated.

Fox News Digital has reached out to reps for Purcell for comment. 

In the midst of his substance abuse and infidelity, Douglas said his first marriage to Diandra Luker eventually came to a head at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel.

After Diandra initially declined to stay with him at the hotel, Douglas called a woman he had been seeing. The woman came to his room, where they had drinks.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Douglas says Diandra unexpectedly returned, obtained a key from the front desk and walked in on them.

"She gave me an ultimatum: ‘Rehab or divorce,’" he writes.

"The indiscretion, the drugs, the booze. I was in a constant state of temporary pleasure or temporary escape," he writes. "In my heart, I knew that I was heading down a very bad road at a very high speed, but I was trying my best to compartmentalize…"

Douglas entered the Sierra Tucson rehabilitation clinic in Arizona in 1992 to receive treatment for alcohol and substance abuse.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Douglas says his rehab stay was later exploited by a tabloid.

He claims two fellow patients sold information about the program to a publication and then left treatment. According to Douglas, the story transformed his treatment for alcohol and drug abuse into a sensational headline portraying him as a sex addict.

"The story that was printed was utter bulls—," Douglas writes. "I had made mistakes, had moments I wasn’t proud of, made choices I wouldn’t have if I wasn’t high, but I was never a f---ing sex addict."

Douglas says the story damaged his reputation and continued to follow him in interviews for decades.

Douglas also writes about an encounter with O.J. Simpson and Rolling Stone co-founder Jann Wenner.

Douglas says he and Wenner encountered Simpson at a "Saturday Night Live" after-party. Wenner invited Simpson back to his apartment, where Simpson allegedly pulled out a rolled dollar bill and offered them cocaine.

"Jann and I were looking at each other — Are we really doing this with O.J. Simpson?" Douglas writes.

He also claims cocaine was readily available throughout Hollywood. Douglas says that at one major talent agency, a valet could allegedly replace a $100 bill left in a car with a packet of cocaine.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Wenner for comment. 

Douglas writes that he spent a private evening with Princess Diana at a London screening of "Wall Street."

He says they sat beside each other during the film, with their hands occasionally touching on the shared armrest. Afterward, they spent time together at a private dinner away from the cameras.

"The truth was simple: she was in an unhappy marriage and wanted a different life," he writes.

He does not claim they had a romantic relationship, but describes their time together as "very special."

Douglas describes his father, Hollywood icon Kirk Douglas, as a powerful, but volatile presence.

"Kirk Douglas was my father, a flawed man with a ferocious temper and a burning ambition," he writes.

Douglas says his father’s behavior left him and his brother Joel frightened. He recalls Kirk saying, "I yell and scream because I care," while Douglas writes that Joel endured more of the abuse.

Douglas says doctors initially treated his persistent throat pain as an infection and prescribed multiple rounds of antibiotics.

A Canadian specialist eventually discovered a subtle swelling at the back of his tongue. A biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma.

"It’s stage IV cancer," the doctor told him, according to Douglas, who says the tumor was the size of a walnut.

Douglas writes that three doctors had missed the cancer and that he had been given the wrong diagnosis for nine months. He feared surgery would require removing part of his tongue and jaw, potentially ending his acting career.

His doctors publicly referred to the disease as throat cancer rather than tongue cancer because they feared reports about possible disfigurement would become sensationalized.

Douglas also describes the darkest years of his son Cameron’s addiction.

"When he was really strung out in New York, I decided I was going to kidnap him and force him into rehab," he writes.

Douglas said that Cameron was addicted to cocaine and heroin, dealt methamphetamine and carried a Glock for protection. During one incident, Cameron flashed the weapon at a drugstore and was nearly shot by police.

At one point, Douglas says he arranged for two large men to help abduct Cameron and force him into rehab.

"When we came back, I asked to hold the leash. Cam figured it out. He looked at me, like, ‘Dad, how could you?’ Like I had broken his heart. Again."

Cameron realized what was happening and resisted, so Douglas threw the plan out of the window.

Cameron later served seven years in prison after a federal drug case. Douglas writes that his son’s heroin relapse behind bars led a judge to add four and a half years to his sentence, and Cameron also spent two years in solitary confinement.

The experience, Douglas writes, forced him to confront his own failures as a father and the destructive cycles that had shaped the Douglas family.

item.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Media skip Mamdani’s ‘genocide’ comment but love him bashing ICE

Israel responded with an all-out military offensive in Gaza that killed more than 70,000 people, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry run by Hamas."

NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK

The evening newscasts on ABC, CBS, and NBC didn’t use any Hamas body counts. But ABC disposed of the subject in a cursory 13 seconds. The other two were somber stories marking the dark day. Targeting kids at Temple Israel in Michigan, a young couple outside the Israeli Embassy in Washington, and a Hanukkah celebration on Australia's Bondi Beach."

The "PBS News Hour" devoted 13 minutes to the anniversary, much of it with Jonathan Dekel-Chen and Jaser Abu Moussa, two men who lost family members on opposite sides of the war, trying to reject hate. They were appearing at the 92nd Street Y in New York that night.

item.title: Discarded trash uncaps 41-year-old murder case in ritzy seaside resort town, authorities say
item.description: A Rhode Island investigator trailed William Morton to a concert and seized a water bottle that allegedly links him to a 1985 Newport murder.
item.content:encoded:
After sitting cold for more than 40 years, a Rhode Island murder case may have been solved with the recovery of a discarded water bottle in a theater.

On Oct. 6, William "Billy" Morton was arrested and charged with first-degree murder for allegedly killing Hillary Hellewell in Newport in 1985.

After four decades, investigators used new DNA technology that allegedly links 61-year-old Morton to the crime.

DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

Since her death, investigators had slowly uncovered clues that suggested Morton might be a suspect. But they needed some of his DNA to confirm the connection.

So in late August, an investigator followed Morton to a Heart tribute band concert at a Rhode Island theater, court records show.

FIANCÉE STICKS BY ACCUSED SERIAL RAPIST AS SPECIAL AGENTS DEFEND TAILING HIM FOR RESTAURANT DNA STAKEOUT

Morton bought popcorn and bottled water for himself and his fiancee, investigators said. But when the couple left the concert early and Morton didn’t pick up his trash, an investigator collected it as potential evidence.

DNA recovered from his water bottle was used to confirm the match to DNA found on Hellewell’s body, according to court documents.

COVERT DNA SAMPLE FROM COLORADO MAN'S TRASH REVIVES 44-YEAR-OLD TEXAS MURDER CASE: REPORT

Morton was taken into custody on Oct. 6. He is being held without bond.

On May 19, 1985, the body of 22-year-old Hellewell was found in Newport, Rhode Island by two brothers – 17 and 20 – who were on their way to work at 4:15 a.m.

Hellewell’s body was lying on a sidewalk along Anthony Street. She was wearing white painter’s pants, a sweater, and socks but no shoes.

Her pulseless body was mostly "cold to the touch," with some areas still "slightly warm" when officers arrived, Morton’s arrest warrant shows.

item.title: Celebrity chef says people have Southern food all wrong, shares what her family ate
item.description: Tiffany Derry challenges Southern food stereotypes, pointing to her Louisiana farm roots and family meals built around fresh vegetables, peas and greens.
item.content:encoded:
Southern food may have a reputation for being heavy and unhealthy, but celebrity chef Tiffany Derry says that stereotype misses a big part of what's traditionally been served on tables across the South.

"I think a lot of times that criticism comes from folks who don't actually understand the South," Derry told Fox News Digital.

The Texas-born chef and restaurateur, who competed on "Top Chef" and recently became a judge on "MasterChef," pointed to her own family's Louisiana roots as an example.

'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS

"We had a farm," she said. "I ate from the farm very much."

Derry said fresh vegetables were a routine part of meals growing up — long before "farm-to-table" became a restaurant buzzword.

"It wasn't this farm-to-table thing. It was what you did," she said.

Neighbors would share what they grew, while meals featured relatively small amounts of protein alongside rice, peas, vegetables and beans, Derry recalled.

DOLLY PARTON'S FAVORITE SOUTHERN DISHES, FROM CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS TO BANANA PUDDING

She said foods commonly associated with Southern cooking today don't tell the entire story.

"It's important to not just tell the story of the country cooking where we talk about mac and cheese and we talk about biscuits and biscuits and gravy," Derry said.

Those heavier dishes represented "such a very small amount of the cooking" and weren't "everyday" foods in her experience.

Cooking was also a family affair. Derry said her grandmother had 11 children and she has more than 50 cousins. As a child, Derry helped prepare greens, peas and green beans.

"People don't really understand where food comes from," she said.

After 27 years in the restaurant industry, however, Derry believes she's seeing renewed interest in cooking at home.

She recalled a period when Americans seemed to be cooking less and some people "just didn't really know how to cook." Now, she said, younger generations are seeking out recipes on TikTok, entertaining at home and even embracing bread-making.

"I love the fact that people are interested in sourdough. Like, are you kidding me?" Derry said. "People are back making bread."

Derry sees the evolution firsthand on "MasterChef," where home cooks can progress to producing food that looks as though it came from professional chefs.

She also noted that some younger cooks learned differently from previous generations.

"So many of their parents didn't really cook," Derry said. "And so they learned on their own, and they learned through watching and through chefs and TV and reading books and magazines and all of that."

Derry spoke with Fox News Digital while promoting a partnership with Tostitos and the brand's new Chunky Guacamole for football season.

She said tailgating food has undergone its own transformation, ranging from traditional burgers to Kobe beef sliders and increasingly elaborate spreads made for Instagram.

"Before, people weren't taking pictures of it. They were just eating it," Derry said.

item.title: World Series champion says potential MLB lockout could 'absolutely' cause cancelled games next season
item.description: World Series champion Nick Swisher said games could "absolutely" be missed next season as MLB and the players association remain far apart on the thought of a salary cap.
item.content:encoded:
In a normal year, most MLB teams would already be looking toward next year at this point in the season, as only a few teams remain alive. But what does next season even look like?

Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association are all but guaranteed to have a lockout beginning Dec. 1 , as both sides have diametrically opposed positions on a salary cap. The owners are pushing hard to implement a salary cap, while the players are vehemently opposed.

World Series champion Nick Swisher said that games could "absolutely" be missed next season due to a stalemate between the two sides.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Absolutely, because just like yourself as me, is all of a sudden, you hear the players association speaking this language and the commissioner's office is speaking this language. I immediately knew out of the gate. Plus, just knowing a little bit more under the hood about the last couple of collective bargaining agreements, right?" Swisher told OutKick in a recent interview.

The former New York Yankees star noted that Tony Clark is no longer the head of the MLBPA after resigning in February and that Bruce Meyer, who took over for Clark, will want everyone to know how he does business. Swisher said he hopes both sides go to the negotiating table in good faith.

"When you get people going to the negotiation table, you're hoping that everyone's trying to go to negotiate a fair deal. You're hoping that both sides aren't trying to go to the negotiation table to win. Because if that's the case, we're in a lot of trouble. Because we're really, really far apart from each other right now, and the last thing we wanna do is slow this train down," Swisher said.

Swisher said baseball is "absolutely crushing" right now, with revenue and attendance both up, going so far as to say that the game has never been in a better place. Yet, having spent 12 seasons in the big leagues, he understands just how tough the union is.

"Pretty much all other sports are very salary cap-based, and that's kind of been the one thing for the players association and the players union. It's one of the strongest unions in the world for a reason, because they stand up for each other. And I was part of that before. I know the bond, I know the brothership, and, listen, it's a tough union," Swisher said.

WILL MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL STILL LOCK PLAYERS OUT AFTER 2026 POSTSEASON PROVES OWNERS WRONG?

Swisher, like the rest of the baseball world, hopes the two sides can reach an agreement before any games are lost .

"I think at the end of the day, man, I'm praying that everything gets itself back on track come the end of the season because I wouldn't wanna slow this train down, man. It's moving too fast right now and we got too many things going on well in our game to be slowing it down right now," Swisher said.

During the Division Series, two prominent players were forced to make an impossible decision: Miss their child's birth or leave their team during the postseason to attend the milestone event?

About an hour before the San Diego Padres faced the Milwaukee Brewers with their season on the line, All-Star closer Mason Miller went on the paternity list to attend the birth of his child. The Padres won Game 3 and staved off elimination in his absence.

New York Yankees starting pitcher Max Fried, on the other hand, said that despite his girlfriend being ready to give birth at any moment, he would pitch in Game 3 no matter what. The Yankees lost the game, so Fried is now free to support his girlfriend for the foreseeable future.

Swisher, a father of two children , said he was fortunate to avoid the dilemma Miller and Fried faced .

"I was very blessed that I had one child that was born at the beginning of the season and one child that was born in the middle of the season. So, I didn't get presented with this situation where both of these individuals are put in," Swisher said.

LEGENDARY SPORTS AGENT WARNS MLB LOCKOUT WOULD BE 'REMARKABLY SELF-DESTRUCTIVE' WITH CBA SET TO EXPIRE

"It's hard for me to say that as a father now of two beautiful young girls that I wouldn't want to be there for the birth of my daughter. But once again, I was never put in that position."

Having played in numerous postseason games, the former All-Star outfielder said it would have been difficult to miss those opportunities .

"At the end of the day, I will tell you this, it's not as often as you think that you get to compete for championships. And for myself, I played in a bunch of playoff games, and we had one great championship run. And it would be really hard for me also to say that I missed out on any of that as well," Swisher said.

While it would be difficult to miss a postseason game, the 45-year-old said he couldn't reconcile missing the birth of one of his children.

"For myself, at the end of the day, I've never been presented with something like that, so, I really wouldn't even know how to answer that because if I missed the birth of my daughters, either one of them. I feel like that would always bother me," Swisher said.

"That would, I would just like – I wasn't there for you. And as a father, that's the one thing that you wanna do is you always wanna be there for your children. So, I can't blame Mason, I can't blame Max."

While fans see the players on the field and managers making lineup and bullpen decisions, much more goes into running a team behind the scenes .

Swisher praised Yankees equipment manager Rob Cucuzza and the entire clubhouse staff for their work.

"At the end of the day, I think the unsung heroes are the clubhouse guys, right? The clubhouse, you know, people that, that clean our underwear, right? That wash our jerseys, right, that are up at 4 o'clock in the morning, just unpacking our bags, getting ourselves ready for the next day's worth of work," Swisher, who spoke on behalf of PAYDAY to highlight the low-key legends who helped shape his career, said.

"If you don't have those people, if you don't have the engine of your organization, you're not gonna be any good. And the fact that we are so blessed to have someone in New York who does that, who does just that, has an amazing job."

item.title: Sally Yates' Cornell alleged gang rape review could scrutinize crucial police interview, attorney says
item.description: Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity case faces fresh scrutiny as Sally Yates examines a key police interview prosecutors never fully received.
item.content:encoded:
A key campus police interview that local prosecutors say they never received in full before initially declining to bring charges in the Cornell University alleged rape case could face fresh scrutiny as former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates reviews the Ivy League school's handling of the allegations.

Yates, who served as deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, has been tapped by Cornell's trustees to conduct a sweeping independent review of the October 2024 allegations involving members of its Chi Phi fraternity, after the university's own investigation resulted in expulsions and suspensions.

The woman, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, told Cornell University Police during a November 2024 interview, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," according to a transcript obtained by CBS News. She also described later sexual activity as coercive and said she had been "completely and totally incapacitated."

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, however, said his office reviewed a six-page sworn statement that described Doe's participation in the sexual activity and drug use as voluntary and consensual.

Van Houten said his office did not initially receive the complete interview and told CBS News last week that the information in the fuller interview "changes the landscape for me."

INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM

Scott Iseman, a New York attorney who has represented students accused of campus sexual misconduct, said Yates could review Doe's full police interview and compare it with her sworn statement, later testimony and other evidence gathered during Cornell's investigation.

"Those full recorded interviews, I can tell you from experience, have a treasure trove of information that are really, really important to exactly what happened," Iseman said.

"It wouldn't surprise me if there was additional information in there that would have changed the trajectory of this case because that happens all the time," he added.

The apparent differences between Doe's full interview and her shorter sworn statement could be particularly significant, Iseman said.

"Law enforcement is supposed to make sure that all salient facts are included in that sworn statement," he said.

Cornell said its police department provided prosecutors with Doe's sworn statement and a Snapchat screenshot in 2024, describing the evidence-sharing process as standard protocol when a possible crime has occurred.

Iseman cautioned that he had not reviewed the complete interview, which has not been made publicly available, and could not determine whether any omitted information was material. It remains unclear why the full interview was not initially provided to Van Houten's office. Fox News Digital reached out to Cornell University Police and the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office for clarification.

Cornell said Yates and her team will have access to relevant records, case files, university personnel and leadership as they review the school's response, under its original Title IX investigation, which determines whether students violated university sexual misconduct policies rather than criminal law.

Beyond the police interview, Iseman said Yates could identify witnesses who were never questioned, overlooked text messages or social media evidence, and other information that did not emerge during Cornell's original investigation.

"There's a lot that potentially she could uncover," Iseman said.

But he cautioned against assuming Cornell mishandled the allegations.

"It may have all been done very appropriately by Cornell. We don't know yet."

CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE

Cornell has defended its handling of the allegations, pointing to an extensive investigation that included more than 50 interviews and 12 days of disciplinary hearings.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said two of the seven accused students were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before discipline could be imposed and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct.

Cornell said both the accuser and accused students had opportunities to review evidence, testify and challenge the findings through an appeals process.

Yates was brought in after the case erupted into a national firestorm following Doe's Sept. 16 lawsuit, which laid out graphic allegations that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her during a night involving alcohol, drugs and group sex at their fraternity house in October 2024. The allegations have since sparked protests on campus while New York Attorney General Letitia James' office is conducting a separate criminal investigation.

The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men.

Yates' investigation extends beyond the Chi Phi case to examine how Cornell handles sexual misconduct allegations across campus, including its oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations.

Her team at law firm King & Spalding will also assess Cornell's practices against federal and state laws and examine whether the university followed its own procedures in responding to the Chi Phi allegations.

Any new or previously overlooked evidence identified during the review could potentially be shared with James' office, Iseman said, though Yates herself has no authority to bring charges.

BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE

Her findings could also lead to recommendations for improving Cornell's procedures, even if the university is found to have followed its existing rules. Cornell said Yates will report her findings and recommendations to a special committee of its Board of Trustees, which intends to share the results with the university community.

Yates has tackled explosive misconduct allegations before.

Her 2022 investigation into women's professional soccer exposed widespread sexual harassment, coercion and abuse by coaches, along with failures by league officials to act on complaints.

What began as an investigation into individual coaches exposed much wider problems across women's soccer, prompting a series of recommendations for sweeping reforms that U.S. Soccer subsequently pledged to implement.

The Cornell case also highlights a wider debate over the legal protections available to students accused of serious sexual misconduct, even as universities have the power to expel them.

John R. Grasso, a Rhode Island criminal defense attorney and former police officer who has represented accused students for two decades, argued that campus disciplinary proceedings can carry life-altering consequences without offering the same legal protections available in criminal court.

"When I defend a student on campus, we don't have any right to discovery. We can't compel the production of anything," Grasso said.

He said those limitations can make it difficult for attorneys to obtain potentially important text messages, photographs and other evidence that might support an accused student's defense.

Grasso also described the difficult choice students can face when university disciplinary proceedings and criminal investigations overlap: participating in campus proceedings and potentially making statements that could affect a criminal case, or remaining silent and risking disciplinary consequences.

"I have a right to remain silent, but if I don't participate, I'm getting found responsible," he said, describing the dilemma he has encountered representing students.

Grasso said the consequences of campus sexual misconduct allegations can extend far beyond disciplinary hearings, describing students whose education, reputations and emotional well-being have suffered even when they were ultimately cleared.

"Bad things happen to the accused the minute a complaint is filed against them on campus. Really bad things," he said.

With the allegations now under renewed scrutiny, Iseman stressed the importance of keeping an open mind about what actually happened.

"Just because the allegations are salacious or dramatic does not mean that's what happened," Iseman said. "So people need to keep an open mind."

item.title: Rahm Emanuel challenges DSA’s influence on Democrats, warns GOP ‘wing’ is disappearing
item.description: Rahm Emanuel warns the Republican Party faces a Mitt Romney and John McCain-style moderate exodus as the Democratic Party debates its left flank.
item.content:encoded:
As Democratic socialists, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, gain ground within the Democratic Party, former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel argued that socialists have less influence over his party than Republicans contend.

Emanuel, the former mayor of Chicago and, at one point, President Barack Obama’s right-hand man, distanced himself from the more radical positions of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) while suggesting that the group could have a place within the party if it adopted more moderate positions.

"I don't believe the socialists are a wing," he told the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "I think they are a separate party. They believe in defunding the police, which is not the party position. They believe open borders and open prisons. That's not the party’s position."

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA

"When you switch that, we can talk," Emanuel added.

Conservatives have expressed concern over the rise of far-left, progressive candidates within the Democratic Party, warning that socialist-leaning politicians like Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., could overtake party moderates.

MAMDANI, TOUTING RI SOCIALIST’S VICTORY, ANSWERS QUESTION OF ‘WHAT IS THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY?’

Emanuel pushed back on the Republican Party’s characterization of the Democratic Party’s trajectory, pointing to New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger as examples of Democratic pragmatism.

"I don't think that's where the party is," Emanuel said. "I think the party is in the pragmatic wing; you can see that in the governor of Virginia, you can see that in the governor of New Jersey, how they both won their primaries."

FORMER DNC VICE CHAIR DAVID HOGG CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC MODERATES 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT VALUES'

The longtime Clinton adviser argued that it is healthy for the Democratic Party to have debate between its progressive and moderate factions. He also warned that the Republican Party faces an exodus of its moderate wing once spearheaded by Mitt Romney and John McCain.

"I happen to think we're going to have a healthy debate in our party," Emanuel told host Sean Hannity. "We haven't had it for 20 years."

JAMES CARVILLE PREDICTS A 2028 'RECKONING' AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATES EYE THE DEMOCRATIC TICKET

"There is a progressive and a pragmatic wing of the party. We'll have a healthy debate. That's what we should have," he continued. "In the same way that the Romney and McCain wing of your party is leaving. They have walked away, and that's what's going to tell the story of 2026."

Emanuel’s comments come as he joins a broader group of establishment Democrats navigating an evolving Democratic Party, where Democratic socialist figures have gained prominence alongside the party’s more moderate tradition.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is turning to former President Bill Clinton as his political model as speculation builds around his potential 2028 presidential bid, telling Vanity Fair Clinton is a "master of his craft."

"I watch videos of Clinton. I seek his counsel, his advice, and even in his absence, do that. I’ve been a student of his from day one," he told the outlet.

item.title: DEPROGRAMMED: How a man radicalized by the Taliban became a counterterrorism force saving lives from extremism
item.description: Mubin Shaikh reveals how the Taliban radicalized him in Pakistan and how marriage and 9/11 sparked his deradicalization and counter-terrorism career.
item.content:encoded:
Mubin Shaikh, a former Jihadist radicalized by the Taliban, details the radicalization process that enamored him with extremist ideology, before he snapped out of those views to become a counter-terrorism specialist for the United States and Canada.

"The biggest indicator [of radicalization is] what we call pathway to violence behaviors. So, doing reconnaissance on a target, looking up, you know, where's the local synagogue? Where's the local mosque?" Shaikh told Fox News Digital.

"It's very important for parents, educators and others to be aware of these signs so that they can possibly prevent the next attack," he continued.

AMERICAN YOUTH RADICALIZED ONLINE, BUSTED IN SUSPECTED TERROR PLOTS AFTER HATING COUNTRY ON SOCIAL MEDIA

Shaikh’s introduction to radicalization began after a house party, where his uncle "guilt tripped" him into thinking the party was the "most heinous thing possible" he could’ve done that "dishonored" his family.

"That’s what made me tell myself, I need to get religious, and that is what would start my radicalization," he continued.

That incident prompted his travels to India, Syria and Pakistan, where he was radicalized by the Taliban.

SHE WAS MARRIED TO AN AL QAEDA MEMBER. NOW ONE WOMAN IS FIGHTING THE TERRORISM SHE SAW UP CLOSE

"The city that I was sent to in Pakistan was called Quetta and was and is a Taliban stronghold… I had a chance encounter with the Taliban who basically impressed upon me that the only way for me to really be successful in this world and the next world was to be a militant, was to fight in jihad," he added.

"Me, [as] this young man looking for a sense of meaning, belonging [and] identity, these guys gave me what I thought I was looking for - and I became a supporter of their mentality," Shaikh continued.

A few years later Shaikh got married — a reality he says started to clear the smoke around his extremist views.

MUSLIM JAIL GANGS SAID TO FORCE CONVERSIONS ON PRISONERS IN UK: 'JIHADIST TRAINING CAMPS’

"The abstract conversations around theology and geopolitics yielded to the very real reality in front of me of having a wife and the idea that I could have a future, I could start a family, and so that became more important for me in my life. And that was basically addressing intimacy needs that every human being has. And so my interest in the extremist world started to wane a bit," he said.

September 11th, 2001 would later become the biggest single catalyst in deradicalizing Shaikh. The worst terrorist attack in American history prompted him to travel to Syria, and research Islamic studies in depth.

"I would spend two years there studying Arabic and Islamic studies and would go through this period of de-radicalization," he continued.

MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD-LINKED NETWORKS EMBEDDED ACROSS CANADIAN INSTITUTIONS, NEW REPORT ALLEGES

When he returned to Canada, "the first Canadian had been arrested on terrorism charges after the newly minted post-9-11 anti-terror legislation" - Momin Khawaja - a fellow classmate and peer of Shaikh from Quran school during his childhood.

Shaikh saw reference to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) and reached out to them, thinking Khawaja’s accusal a mistake. Once they confirmed his classmate’s arrest and spoke more to Shaikh, CSIS recruited him as an undercover operative in counterterrorism efforts.

"I was already online, looking at the extremism that was out there… and by 2012, started to see the rise of ISIS in real time. It was at this time that the US government reached out to me and said, 'Hey, can you help us out with what's coming?' And so from 2012 to 2020, I participated and I supported the coalition against ISIS in various anti-ISIS activities and operations," he continued.

HEZBOLLAH GROOMS CHILDREN FOR MARTYRDOM THROUGH ITS SCOUT MOVEMENT, REPORT CLAIMS

Shaikh works now as an exit peer specialist for Parents for Peace, a nonprofit fighting radicalization and extremism by intervening with individuals before it’s too late, most of whom "overwhelmingly are juveniles" under 18.

"What gives me hope in countering extremism is really seeing how people turn out after they've left extremist ideologies. It's like a night-and-day difference. And when they come to see the mistake that they were making, when they come to see the pathway that it was leading them towards and seeing that they have left that, their lives get better, their personal situation gets better," he continued.

"To see parents, you know, have their kid back again — that's what it's all about," Shaikh said.

item.title: America's truckers issue dire warning as soaring diesel costs threaten 'domino effect'
item.description: Truckers say diesel at $6.32 per gallon is slashing profits and cutting routes, warning of a domino effect that could ripple through the supply chain.
item.content:encoded:
American truckers are warning that sky-high diesel prices are eating into their profits and putting pressure on trucking companies to cut routes, raising concerns that some drivers could be forced off the road and the pain could eventually reach Americans at the grocery store.

"Fuel prices is going up, the rates are not going up," Miami-based trucker Suave Dorsett told Fox News Digital. "So it's hurting our pockets real bad."

The warnings come as the Iran war sends diesel prices soaring, squeezing American truckers even as President Donald Trump predicts oil prices will fall "like a stone" amid expectations that the conflict could soon end. Drivers told Fox News Digital the damage is already mounting, with routes being cut and smaller operators facing mounting financial pressure.

Dorsett is among several truckers who told Fox News Digital that soaring fuel costs are cutting into their earnings and putting pressure on an industry responsible for moving goods across the country, with one driver reporting fewer routes and others warning that smaller operators could eventually be forced to park their rigs.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

The national average for diesel stood at roughly $6.32 per gallon Monday, according to AAA — up from about $3.69 at the same time last year, a jump of more than 70%. The surge has also eclipsed the previous record of $5.816 per gallon, set in June 2022 under former President Joe Biden as Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent global energy prices soaring.

For Dorsett, who has been driving for nine years, the price at the pump was even steeper. He told Fox News Digital he was seeing diesel at $7.40 per gallon while traveling through Ohio.

Dorsett said the fuel spike comes as truckers are already shouldering a long list of expenses, including diesel exhaust fluid (DEF), which helps reduce harmful emissions, parking, showers, weighing and reweighing loads, repairs and towing.

And if diesel prices remain elevated, Dorsett predicted smaller operators will be the first to buckle.

BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK

"Some of the smaller companies, like the smaller owner ops, would slowly fall off and it's going to create a chain effect," Dorsett said, predicting a "domino effect" that could eventually put pressure on larger carriers.

Tyler Rinaldi, a Louisiana trucker with about a decade of experience who transports hazardous materials and other freight for an LTL company, said he has already seen weekend routes scaled back at his company.

"I've seen a lot of routes get cut," Rinaldi told Fox News Digital. "They're not really running like they want to on the weekends right now."

"I definitely see a lot change because of it at my company, slowly, but it's starting to be more noticeable," he added.

TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS

Rinaldi, who is married with two children, said fewer routes could eventually mean less money coming home.

"When they start cutting routes and trying to limit the expenses on what routes they send out," Rinaldi said, "that takes away from the people that work in the company's pockets."

Avante Jackson, an 11-year trucking veteran from Charlotte, North Carolina, who transports steel and other construction materials, said rising diesel prices are forcing truckers to take a harder look at whether the money they bring in is enough to keep their businesses running.

"If I'm putting all of my profit in the tank," Jackson said, "at the end of the day, what do I have left to keep the doors open?"

CUT THE BULL: THE REAL REASON BEEF COSTS SO MUCH — AND WHAT TRUMP IS TRYING TO DO

Jackson cautioned against "fear-mongering" about potential shortages, but said a widespread loss of drivers could ultimately reach consumers.

"It really could hit the community," he said.

The latest diesel spike echoes a similar crunch in 2022 under former President Joe Biden, when the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent fuel prices flying. Diesel reached a then-record national average of $5.82 per gallon that June, squeezing truckers as operating expenses climbed.

According to the American Transportation Research Institute, trucking fuel costs surged 53.7% in 2022, helping drive a 21.3% jump in overall operating costs to a then-record $2.25 per mile. The latest spike threatens to revive those pressures, particularly for smaller operators with less room to absorb rising fuel bills.

As the Trump administration pushes international partners to release emergency fuel reserves in an effort to bring prices down, the truckers had their own message for the president: don't forget about the drivers absorbing the costs on the road.

"My message to President Trump would just be to think about who's keeping America moving," Jackson told Fox News Digital. "Think about the little guys out here each and every day."

TRUMP JUST BROKERED A DEAL WITH THE COUNTRY SITTING ATOP THE WORLD’S LARGEST OIL RESERVES

"We truly are the backbone of America, we keep America moving," he added. "We just want you just to think about us and put yourself in our shoes...Let's try to get the fuel prices down and let's try to just make more of a change," he said. "We know we can do better."

Trump defended higher fuel prices Thursday as a temporary sacrifice in the fight to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, saying on Truth Social that rising gasoline costs were "a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon."

Trump said last week that European countries had agreed to release diesel from their stockpiles after he pressed them to put more supply on the market. The G7 subsequently agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products from previously pledged emergency reserves over four months, including a substantial diesel release during the first 20 days, in an effort to ease pressure on global fuel markets.

Trump also said his administration would not pursue a diesel export ban and expressed confidence that oil prices would eventually return to levels seen before the latest spike, though energy markets remain under pressure from global supply disruptions.

Trump predicted during a Wednesday night rally in San Antonio, Texas, that oil prices would "come down like a rock" once the war with Iran ends, insisting the conflict would be over "very soon."

"This week, President Trump signed an executive order that will quickly cut diesel costs and put money directly back into the pockets of American truckers, saving them over $100 every time they refill at the gas pump. Last week, he negotiated a deal with our European counterparts to release 100 million barrels—mainly diesel—from their stockpiles to add supply to the market and lower costs," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

"The President wants to see prices at the pump fall and continues to take historic action to ease temporary disruptions as oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz approaches pre-conflict levels," Rogers added.

item.title: Veteran shot 7 times in Fort Hood massacre has a warning for Americans planning to watch execution
item.description: A Fort Hood shooting survivor shot seven times by Nidal Hasan wants to witness the firing squad execution but warns against treating it as a spectacle.
item.content:encoded:
On Dec. 3, 2026, the U.S. government intends to take Nidal Hasan to a firing range at Fort Hood and publicly execute him.

Few condemned men could make a more difficult case for mercy.

Seventeen years ago, Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time, walked into a soldier readiness center at the Texas Army post and opened fire, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. Now, after years of appeals, the Army is preparing to execute him by firing squad.

And Americans will be able to watch on live stream.

That last detail has transformed what might otherwise have been the long-delayed conclusion of one of the darkest chapters in the Army's history into a more uncomfortable question: How should a nation reckon with the gravity of taking a life, even when that life belongs to a mass murderer?

For Alonzo Lunsford, a former Army staff sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan, the answer is complicated.

GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT

Lunsford wants Hasan executed. He intends to witness it himself in December. He told Fox News Digital he would even prefer that one of Hasan's surviving victims or the relatives of those he killed be allowed to pull the trigger.

Despite that, Lunsford says he has forgiven Hasan.

"The weird thing about it, I've forgiven him because my faith does not allow me to heal and continue unless I forgive that man," Lunsford said.

But forgiveness, for Lunsford, does not mean sparing Hasan from punishment. What troubles him is the prospect of turning that punishment into entertainment.

"It's not a spectacle," he said. "There's nothing glorified in the smell of human flesh, blood and gunpowder. It's a smell you will never forget. It's a taste that you will never forget."

"That's not something you sit around and say, hey, let's get some popcorn and look at this execution," he continued. "We as a people, we're better than that. This ain't no country where we do public beheadings and stonings and think it's fine."

ARMY SERGEANT SENTENCED AFTER SHOOTING 5 SOLDIERS AND HIS MALE FIANCÉ AT FORT STEWART

Lunsford was working at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center on Nov. 5, 2009, when Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, opened fire. He recalled watching Hasan kill a colleague before turning the weapon on him. Lunsford was shot above his left eye, fell to the floor and played dead before eventually escaping outside, where Hasan shot him again.

"I've accepted the fact I'm gonna live with the pain for the rest of my life," Lunsford said.

He has since found purpose in coaching basketball, mentoring young people and helping others struggling with their mental health.

Lunsford said he doesn't want children watching the livestream, though he believes adults can decide for themselves whether to tune in.

"This is not somewhere you all start throwing some meat on the grill, get outside and say, hey, we're gonna watch them unalive this guy by firing squad," he said. "Don't do that."

"Don't do that because when you do that, you're dishonoring those that made the supreme sacrifice, those who are no longer here. Those are heroes."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended making the execution public, saying Americans should understand the consequences of Hasan's crimes.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said in an interview this week. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."

Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon would follow through with its plans to livestream Hasan's execution, saying he had no intention of watching it himself.

"I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he told reporters Friday.

The decision for the first U.S. Army death by firing squad in 86 years to be live streamed has drawn opposition even from Republicans who support putting Hasan to death.

"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote on X.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., likewise said Hasan "should face the death penalty," but called publicly streaming it "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

The nation's Catholic bishops have gone further, opposing both Hasan's execution and the decision to make it public. "In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, said Friday.

"The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

The decision has also raised a more immediate national security concern.

Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot during the 2009 attack, has previously spoken about becoming a martyr. Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury counterterrorism official and director of the Washington Institute's Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, warned that making footage of his death widely available could give terrorist groups material to exploit.

"It seems like a poor decision to provide terrorist groups with a video clip they can effectively splice into radicalization propaganda," Levitt told Fox News Digital.

"There's no tangible benefit to live streaming an execution, and it may, in fact, exacerbate the terrorist threat."

For Lunsford, however, the execution remains deeply personal.

During Hasan's 2013 court-martial, the two locked eyes. Lunsford wants Hasan to see him again before he dies.

"I want to look at him in his eyes. I want him to see me — man to man," Lunsford said. "My message to him: Dude, you failed."

"I go where I wanna go, when I wanna go, how I wanna go. With no fear," he said. "I can go outside and just smell and listen to nature. You don't have that luxury."

And despite everything Hasan took from him, Lunsford said he hopes the condemned man uses his final moments to repent.

"I want to give him the opportunity to, the last words out of his mouth is to apologize and repent," Lunsford said. "And be held accountable for his sins and for his crime. And I will be OK with that."

item.title: ‘Donroe’ Doctrine and conservative victories squeeze cartels in Latin America
item.description: The Sinaloa cartel and CJNG are rapidly adapting as Trump's Shield of the Americas coalition squeezes drug trafficking routes across the hemisphere.
item.content:encoded:
The cartels are losing political cover, and they know it.

The Trump administration has treated the Western Hemisphere as a security problem — rather than allow diplomatic courtesy to block needed action. Venezuelan strongman Nicolás Maduro is in U.S. custody. Colombia elected Abelardo de la Espriella, who ran against negotiations with armed groups and won. Argentina, Chile, Ecuador, Paraguay and others have aligned with Washington’s enforcement policies. The Shield of the Americas coalition now coordinates intelligence and operations against cartel networks – but with a handful of exceptions: Mexico, Brazil, Cuba and Nicaragua.

That is the Donroe Doctrine in practice: American predominance in the hemisphere, applied to migration, Chinese footholds and the drug trade.

EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY

Critically, this is a major shift in the operating environments for the Sinaloa cartel, CJNG (Jalisco New Generation Cartel), and the Colombian and Venezuelan networks that fed them.

Cuba is the weakest link in the old arc. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the regime has already fallen as a functioning state. About a fifth of the population has left since 2021. The lights fail, the peso is worthless and the government that remains specializes in jailing people. Whether the Castro apparatus collapses by December is unknowable. What is knowable is that Havana is no longer a reliable logistics or intelligence partner for anyone who needs one.

In Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Morena government is increasingly alone. It keeps bilateral contacts with Washington while refusing the regional coalition, citing fear of U.S. operations on Mexican soil. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins the Brazilian runoff, Sheinbaum’s remaining major left-of-center counterpart in the region is gone. Isolation raises the diplomatic cost of open sanctuary to the drug lords.

But the cartels are already adjusting.

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

In August, Spanish police rolled up a CJNG-linked cell that moved roughly 2.5 tons of methamphetamine dissolved in vanilla aroma and finished it in a lab in Lleida. Earlier Sinaloa shipments concealed in marble statues met the same end. Mexican groups are treating Europe as a synthetics market precisely because cocaine corridors face more hostile governments.

Colombia’s new president has ended the prior administration’s accommodation with armed actors. Venezuelan airspace and ports, long protected by the Cartel de los Soles network, are under direct U.S. pressure. U.S. strikes on drug running fast boats have sharply reduced Eastern Caribbean drug traffic. Routes move. Chemistry is portable — coca fields aren’t.

TRUMP ALLY 'EL TIGRE' SWORN IN AS COLOMBIA'S NEW PRESIDENT AMID CONTINENT'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT

Violence is scaling with the same logic. Mexican authorities have arrested clusters of former Colombian soldiers — nine of 12 in one Michoacán case were ex-military — after mine attacks that killed Mexican troops. These men are hired for ambush drills, explosives and drone work. They are not a kill team loyal to former Colombian President Gustavo Petro; Petro is out of office. They are mercenaries. Cartels pay for skills the Mexican state has not matched.

The drone piece is further along than most reporting admits. Cartel explosives drops from commercial quadcopters are already routine. French and U.S. defense outlets have documented Mexican and Colombian nationals entering Ukraine’s International Legion, some with fraudulent papers, seeking assignment to First-Person View (FPV) units. One alias, Águila-7, drew instructor suspicion in Lviv for technical proficiency inconsistent with a humanitarian volunteer. The skills learned on a brutal battlefield transfer seamlessly to the Western Hemisphere.

CRIME, KIDNAPPINGS AND DRONE ATTACKS FLAGGED IN US WARNING FOR BORDER REGION

And a prosecutor’s office in Tijuana has already been hit by nail-packed drones. Border sightings run into the tens of thousands. The February El Paso airspace closure was the public admission of a problem that has been operational for years.

With the cartels being squeezed, three shifts are likely.

WATCH: DHS ISSUES STARK WARNING AFTER 300 ‘HOSTILE’ CARTEL DRONES DETECTED AT SOUTHERN BORDER

First, more "legitimate" business. Avocado orchards, fuel theft, mining extortion and chemical import fronts are already balance-sheet items. European logistics firms and real-estate laundering are the export version. Synthetics let production move to whatever jurisdiction still looks the other way.

Second, sharper violence where territory is contested. Leadership disruption and route competition have historically produced spikes in ambushes, not quiet consolidation. Armored "monstruo" trucks, landmines and FPV drones lower the cost of killing rivals and local police. Expect more of it in Michoacán, Jalisco and the border plazas.

TRUMP CAN PROTECT CALIFORNIA AVOCADO FARMERS AND TAKE A BITE OUT OF MEXICAN CARTELS, TOO

Third, heavier investment in bribery and extortion of officials on both sides of the border. Lost geographic sanctuary makes a compromised port inspector, financial regulator or federal agent more valuable. This is old cartel practice. The premium on it rises when the political umbrellas fold.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

None of this requires a Cuban collapse date or proof that Petro-era Colombian special forces are running kill teams for the cartels. Latin America’s electoral realignment, the U.S. maritime campaign, the European meth seizures, the foreign-fighter drone pipeline and Mexico’s narrowing diplomatic company are enough.

Cartels are businesses under pressure. They will trade some territory for laboratories, drones and officials who can be bought or frightened. The test is whether the Shield of the Americas coalition raises those costs faster than the cartels and their corrupted political patrons can reroute.
